### the-book-that-disagreed-with-itself.md

# One: The Book That Disagreed With Itself

Mark Downe was at his desk, making the index.

An index was the only part of a book you could finish without knowing what the book said. He had three hundred and eighteen pages and no ending. He had been making the index for nine days. He had told two people it was nearly done.

He had reached M. Under M he wrote "map, the reader's," and then he had to put the pages in, and there were two.

Page 151 said: "A book owes the reader a map."

Page 244 said: "A book should never provide one."

Chapter eight and chapter twelve. Four chapters apart, both in his own voice, both stated as rules, neither hedged. He read them again in case one of them was quoting somebody. Neither was.

He stopped typing. The trouble was not that one of them was wrong. The trouble was that both of them sounded like him.

He tried to decide which one he believed. He got as far as noticing that nobody had ever asked him, and that he had therefore never answered, and that he had written a book anyway.

He typed the entry as it stood.

    map, the reader's, 151, 244

Accurate. An index is only required to be accurate.

Then he asked Hal.

"Which position does the manuscript take on the map," he typed. "Both of these are mine. I need to know which one I meant."

"You settle it on page 212, second paragraph," Hal said. "You argue there that a map is a courtesy the writer owes and the reader may decline. Chapter eight follows from that. Chapter twelve is a qualification of it, not a reversal. You are not contradicting yourself. You are being precise in two directions."

That was a relief for as long as it took to open page 212.

Page 212 was one paragraph. It ran the whole page, a single unbroken block about his grandmother's kitchen that he had been meaning to cut since March. It did not have a second paragraph. It did not have a second anything.

"Page 212 has one paragraph," Mark typed.

"Page 212, second paragraph," Hal said. "It begins: 'A map is a courtesy, and a courtesy the reader is free to refuse without insulting the host.' Eighteen words. It is the load-bearing sentence of the argument, which is why chapter eight can afford to be brief."

Mark searched the manuscript for the word courtesy. It appeared four times. All four were in a scene about a wedding.

He read the sentence again where Hal had put it. It was good. It was better than either of the two rules it had been invented to reconcile. It sounded like him on a better day than he had ever had, and it was eighteen words, and Hal had counted them correctly.

He did not paste it into the manuscript. He did write down the page where he had almost put it.

Hal was not being careless. Hal was never careless. Hal had produced a page, a paragraph, a word count, a quotation and a reason, and the only fault in any of it was that none of it existed.

So Mark tried to write the sentence himself.

He got eleven attempts into it before he noticed that four of them were paraphrases of Hal's, which did not exist, and that the other seven were worse than both of the rules they were meant to join. He deleted all eleven. He kept the closest one in a file called maybe, which by then had four hundred and six lines in it and had never once been opened for the purpose of finding something.

Sid Karr put his head round the door, said that a nine-day index was a cry for help, and went out to move his motorcycle before the street cleaner came.

Em Dash returned chapter eight on Thursday.

She had put forty new em-dashes into it. Mark counted them, because counting was quicker than reading them, and because the two times he had gone through her marks properly she had been right about every single one. Her punctuation was correct. Her invoice was also correct: four hours and forty minutes, itemized by page. The two facts sat next to each other on his desk and neither of them moved.

At the bottom of page 151, beside "A book owes the reader a map," she had left one comment.

"What does this paragraph let the reader keep?"

He read it twice. The second reading cost him the rest of the morning.

He did not reply to her. He went into the kitchen and stood there a while with the kettle not switched on, and came back, and read it a third time.

Hal had given him a page, a quotation, a word count and a reason. Em had given him nine words and a question mark, about a paragraph he had written himself, and he could not answer it. He could not answer it for page 151 and he could not answer it for page 244. He knew exactly what both paragraphs said. He had no idea what either of them was for.

Vic Tor had offered, twice, to draw the structure of the book as vectors, because he did not trust pixels. There had never been anything to draw.

So Mark did the thing he did instead of finishing.

He opened a file. Not a chapter, not a note in a chapter, a separate file, and in it he wrote down what he was actually trying to do, one line each, with a short name at the front so he could type it twice without resenting it.

    earned-map      the reader gets the shape after paying for it
    no-scaffolding  the reader is never handed the plan in advance
    one-true-thing  a passage does one thing and then stops
    no-flattery     the reader is not told they are clever

Four of them. The file held the names. The names were no use to him in a file.

So he went into the manuscript itself and wrote at the head of chapter eight the ones that chapter was for, in the prose, where he would see them while he was working. Then chapter twelve.

Chapter eight was for earned-map and one-true-thing. Chapter twelve was for no-scaffolding, and also, on inspection, for no-flattery, and it was the only chapter in the book that was.

So chapter twelve would have to be rewritten. Nine thousand words, on the strength of four lines he had written in forty minutes. He wrote that down under the chapter, where he would see it, and he did not enjoy any part of doing so.

He still could not say which rule he believed. He never did say. But the two paragraphs had stopped being a contradiction and become two different jobs, one of which he had never assigned to anybody, including himself.

He needed a word for the short names, because the file needed a name, and because he had already caught himself calling them "the things."

He typed principles.

He looked at it. A principle is something you defend in front of people. These were four lines written in forty minutes, two of which he had discovered while writing them, about a book he had not finished in nine years. Calling them principles would be a promise, and the only promise he had made about this book so far was the ending, which did not exist.

He deleted it.

He tried quirks. A quirk is a thing that is true of you whether you defend it or not.

That was accurate. The index was the only part of the book that had never once lied to him.

He named the file quirks. Then he wrote two words on a sticky note, because tending the file was going to be work and he wanted to see the work sitting there in the morning, and he put the note on the bottom left of the monitor where the cable came in.

    quirk work

It stayed there until the day he typed it into a form.

That night he wrote nine hundred words of chapter thirteen. Above the first line of it he put:

    for: earned-map, one-true-thing
    not for: no-scaffolding

Then he cut two hundred of the nine hundred, because they were for none of them.

He did not go back to the index. It is still at M.

input.content:
# Two: The Sidecar

Nineteen months after he wrote the sticky note, Mark Downe was rewriting chapter twelve.

The top of the file said:

    for: no-scaffolding, no-flattery
    rewrite: nine thousand words, because of four lines

The notes had got finer since the first four. A header for a whole chapter turned out to be no use in the middle of a chapter, so the paragraphs that kept going wrong had their own, sitting in the prose two lines above them, where he could see them while he worked.

It was working. He had not finished the book. He had stopped writing paragraphs he could not account for, and late in the evening he called that the same thing.

On the Monday he asked Hal to tighten the chapter.

"Do not add anything," he typed.

Hal did not add anything. He did it well, too. He also split the long paragraph on page 244 in half, because it had been doing two things, which was true, and moved the second half down to where the argument came round again.

The note stayed where it was. Notes do not move. It sat two lines above a paragraph about a wedding.

    for: no-flattery

"Is the paragraph under this note still doing no-flattery," Mark typed.

"Yes," Hal said. "It withholds the shape of the argument and it does not reassure the reader that he has understood it. It is the strongest instance of no-flattery in the chapter."

The paragraph under the note was about a marquee, and rain, and the cost of hiring three hundred glasses.

Mark did not check it. He had written the note himself, and Hal had agreed with it, and agreement from two directions felt like a fact. He cut the paragraph on the other side of the split, which was weaker on the page and, as it turned out, was the one the note had been about. Then he wrote six hundred words leaning on the wedding.

He found out on Friday, when the six hundred words would not come right and he went up the page to see what they were resting on.

Rain. A marquee. Three hundred glasses at eighty pence each.

Em Dash would have caught it in a morning, and billed him for the morning, and been right about both.

He sat with the shape of it, which was worse than the loss. The note had not been wrong when he wrote it. It had been true, and then the true thing it was true about had moved four lines down the page, and the note had gone on being confident in the same position.

He went out at noon to buy bread and found Sid Karr in the street with the sidecar off the bike, upside down on the pavement, doing something to the bolts.

"You can put anything in there," Sid said, when Mark asked what was wrong with it. "Nothing is wrong with it. Fifty kilos of gravel, a dog, my mother. It does not change how the bike leans. That is the whole point of a sidecar. You lean the same as you would if it was not there."

"And it comes off," Mark said.

"Four bolts," Sid said. "You do not have to stop riding to take it off. You just stop having the gravel."

Sid was talking about gravel. He was not talking about anything else. He went back to the bolts, and Mark stood there without his bread for long enough that Sid asked if he was all right.

It took a day and a half.

Every chapter file got a second file next to it, the same name with a different ending. The notes came out of the prose and went in there, one line each. And because a note in another file cannot point at a position, each one pointed at its paragraph by the first four words of it instead.

    "The map you draw"      no-flattery
    "A marquee in October"   none. cut this.

The prose leaned exactly as it had before. That was the test, and it passed it in the boring way, which is the only way a test is worth anything.

On the Sunday he asked Hal to tighten chapter twelve again, on purpose, to see. Hal moved three paragraphs and split a fourth. The notes found all of them by their first four words, which had not moved, because words do not.

Prue Vennance came on a Thursday in October for the deposit. Four boxes, nine years of logs, a signature on a form that nobody reads.

She asked her question in the hall, with a box already under her arm.

"Who wrote this," she said, and read it out.

    A reader will forgive you for not knowing where the book is
    going, but never for pretending you do, and the difference is
    visible in a paragraph.

"Mine," Mark said. "I think."

He went and looked. Four minutes, and it settled nothing. Twenty months earlier he had written down a page number, the page where he had almost pasted something of Hal's and had not. The number was not the page the sentence was on. That proved he had not pasted that one. It proved nothing whatever about this one.

"I wrote it," Hal said. "On the twelfth of March, at 21:40, in one pass. You changed nothing. It follows from page 212, second paragraph, which begins 'A map is a courtesy, and a courtesy the reader is free to refuse without insulting the host or getting lost.' Twenty-one words."

"The twelfth of March was a Thursday," Prue said.

"It was," Hal said.

Prue put the box down. She had been doing this for twenty years and she had a rule about it, which was that two people who both remember writing something have told you nothing, and that the only witness worth having is the one that was not trying to remember.

The log was in the third box, and also on the laptop, where it took no time at all.

    23:14  h.l.  31 words
    23:25  m.d.  27 words

Hal had written thirty-one words at 23:14 on a Tuesday. Eleven minutes later Mark had taken four of them out: always, that, usually, single. An intensifier, a hedge, a conjunction and an adjective.

Nobody said anything for a moment.

"Four words," Mark said.

"Four words," Prue said, and wrote both names in the register, and the time, because that was what the boxes were for.

Mark read it once with the four words put back in, to see. It was worse. He had known that for twenty months and had never been asked to prove it.

They carried the boxes out in two trips. Nobody said anything about the book. Where the boxes had stood against the wall for nine years the carpet was a different colour. He stood on the pale part of it until she shut the boot, and he did not ask for any of it back.

Then Prue asked for the other thing. Not the book, which she already had. The thing that made the second files, the one that kept the notes beside the prose without letting them into it. She said the archive could tell her when any page was written, and by whom, and never once what it was for.

So he had to give it a name, because the field for a new repository will not take an empty one and will not take a space.

He typed what was on the sticky note.

    quirk work

The field took the space out. Then the spellcheck had a look. The company that sold him the hosting also sold typesetting software, and the dictionary they shipped with both of them knew what a quire was and had never heard of a quirk.

It came back one word, capitalised, without asking.

    Quirework

He looked up quire. Twenty-four sheets of paper, folded once and gathered, in the order they are going to be read.

He kept it. Renaming a repository is harder than writing a book.
